By spending extended time in specific environments, Le Coq captures how landscapes influence his mood, finding that each tree possesses its own "personality" and changes his feelings. Shot across France, Central America, and Asia, the black-and-white images emphasize the symmetry of branches reaching the sky, serving as an opportunity for the viewer to pause and focus on their own individual journeys.

However, she has since rebuilt a determined life, working full-time and advocating as a public speaker to inspire others who look "visibly different." After being formally adopted by Tina and Rog Thomas, Mui manages her rare genetic condition through rigorous daily skincare routines and has become recognized as potentially the fourth oldest person alive with the condition.

The 69th Tony Award nominations were announced Tuesday morning, with Mary-Louise Parker unveiling the nominees alongside Bruce Willis. The ceremony is set to take place June 7 at 8 p.m. on CBS, hosted by Alan Cumming and Kristin Chenoweth. The full list of Best Play and Best Musical nominees includes titles such as "The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time," "Disgraced," "Hand to God," and "Wolf Hall Parts One & Two."

Libyan Army head General Khalifa Haftar has rejected any EU military intervention in Libya, stating his country was not consulted and would not cooperate with such operations. He argued that military action would be unwise and that the EU must respect Libya's sovereignty while addressing the migration crisis through diplomatic means rather than force. Haftar insisted that lifting sanctions on the Libyan army is a necessary condition for any cooperation, framing the issue as a broader Libyan crisis rather than a mere migrant flow.

Mayor Enrique Serrano has launched a tourism campaign to lure foreign investors and tourists back to the city, citing the "30 million legal crossings" across the border as proof of its improving safety. While the Obama administration welcomed Abe to strengthen the U.S.-Japan alliance and the Trans-Pacific Partnership, his revisionist views have undermined trilateral security cooperation with South Korea and China. Despite Abe expressing "everlasting condolences" for American lives, his stance is seen as a retreat from post-era remements, hindering the test of true statesmanship.

Hundreds of decomposed corpses were discovered in shallow graves and on the streets of Damasak, Nigeria, following the recapture of the town from Boko Haram. A provincial committee and local residents, who recovered over 400 bodies, documented the scale of atrocities committed by the group during their occupation. The discovery highlights the extensive destruction and mass graves left behind as Boko Haram's retreat, part of a broader regional military offensive.

Israeli airstrikes in the Golan Heights targeted a group of militants allegedly attempting to plant a bomb on the border with Israel from Syria. The Israeli military reported that three attackers were killed and the device was prevented from being detonated against IDF forces. The incident occurred in internationally recognized occupied territory, where Israel seized land from Syria during the 1967 war.

Two decades later, the FBI continues to prioritize preventing "homegrown attacks" by tracking domestic terrorists ranging from white supremacists to eco-terrorists, though figures like Eric Rudolph and Ted Kaczynski have historically evaded capture. A prosecutor has dropped the case against Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner regarding allegations of a cover-up in the 1994 bombing case. The move by prosecutor Javier de Luca, who found no evidence of a crime, could end the long-standing accusations that have roiled the nation. The case stems from the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community center, where Alberto Nisman had claimed the government struck a deal to shield Iranian suspects before his death.

South Africa celebrated Freedom Day on April 27, marking 30 years since the end of apartheid and the election of Nelson Mandela as president. The occasion was marred by anti-immant attacks earlier in the month that claimed numerous lives, prompting condemnation on social platforms like Twitter. Despite the violence, global figures like Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Google honored the day with doodles, while many South Africans used the hashtag to remember icons like Mandela and express their views on the state of the nation.

A major earthquake struck Kathmandu, Nepal, causing widespread destruction and triggering numerous aftershocks. Survivors gathered in open spaces like fields and crossroads while the historic temples, palaces, and the Kasthamandap temple were reduced to rubble. Am chaos and ongoing aftershocks, people searched for survivors and attempted to reach safety, with communication disrupted but texts and data eventually getting through.

Huge NATO military exercises, code-named "Joint Warrior," are currently underway off and around Britain's coast, involving over 13,000 personnel from 14 countries. NATO insists the drills are a timely response to Russia's increasingly aggressive behavior, rather than a deliberate provocation, as the alliance has been condemning Moscow's actions in Ukraine for over a year. Anamarie Shreeves, a 26-year-old Atlanta resident, has lived nearly zero-waste for six months, generating only a small amount of trash that fits in a mason jar. She adopted this lifestyle after being inspired by a "No Trash Project" blog post and an Ecuadorian sojourn, committing to rigorous preparation—carcling reusable containers and cloth—to avoid the typical consumer waste stream.

Mocha, a Doberman, underwent emergency surgery after ingesting a pile of watch heads, leather straps, and metal pieces, which veterinarians removed during an endoscopy. The owners were shocked by the extent of the items consumed, but the hospital noted that Mocha was stable and recovering as of Friday.

An unmanned Russian Progress spacecraft lost contact with controllers shortly after launch, causing it to spin out of control. NASA and Roscosmos confirmed the vehicle will re-enter Earth's atmosphere between May 5 and May 7, posing no threat to the ISS crew despite the loss of critical cargo. Russia is preparing a replacement launch later this year to resume supply missions to the station.

Photographer Kate Parker created the "Strong is the New Pretty" project to capture her daughters and their friends embracing authentic, active childhoods, moving away from traditional, polished ideals of girlhood. The series features unposed, high-energy moments of girls engaging in sports, nature, and play, aiming to preserve their confidence and curiosity before they lose that sense of self-worth. Ultimately, Parker hopes the work inspires both parents and children to celebrate their individuality and adventurous spirits.

Adult coloring books are rapidly dominating bestseller lists, transitioning from a niche activity for children into a mainstream stress-reduction trend for grownups. Driven by online access and a desire to "unplug" from screens, titles like Johanna Basford's "Secret Garden" and Emma Farrarons "Mindfulness Colouring Book" are flying off shelves as adults rediscover the therapeutic benefits of coloring to unwind. The trend shows no signs of slowing, with new releases and high demand signaling a lasting shift in the market.

A major study reveals a significant rise in heavy and binge drinking across American adults between 2005 and 2012, with heavy drinking increasing by 17.2% and binge drinking rates climbing sharply, particularly among women. Researchers attribute the surge to shifting social norms, noting that in some areas, women's binge drinking rates rose nearly 36% compared to a 23% increase among men, and that nationwide, women's binge drinking increased more than seven times the rate of men's. Roseanne Barr has revealed she is slowly going blind due to macular degeneration, attributing her condition to smoking marijuana, which she believes relieves eye pressure. Despite doctors giving her no definitive timeline, she attended the Tribeca Film Festival in support of her documentary "Roseanne for President!" while making light quips about her deteriorating vision.

Hawaii is poised to become the first state to prohibit tobacco sales to anyone under 21, having raised the minimum legal age from 18. The bill, which awaits Governor Governor David Ige's signature to take effect January 1, 2016, aims to reduce youth smoking and save lives, aligning with a report predicting significant public health benefits if the minimum age were raised nationwide. Jean Nidetch, the founder of Weight Watchers, passed away at the age of 91. She pioneered the weight-loss industry by emphasizing accountability and peer support after her own struggles with fad diets. Her legacy, which began in her New York living room in 1961, has positively impacted the health and well-being of millions worldwide.

Roseanne Barr revealed she is going blind due to two progressive eye diseases, macular degeneration and glaucoma, which are causing her central and peripheral vision loss respectively. Doctors note that the combination of these conditions is "terrible," and while there is no cure, treatments can delay progression; she manages symptoms using marijuana to lower eye pressure. The risk for both diseases increases after age 60, and experts recommend early baseline eye exams starting at age 40 to mitigate vision loss.

Golfers are increasingly turning to yoga to improve their game, focusing on specific movements like mid-back mobility and hip rotation to prevent injury. Professional golfers like Jordan Spieth demonstrate that integrating core strength and functional movement—rather than compensating with the low back—is essential for power and fluidity. The article provides specific yoga-based exercises designed to address these key areas, aiming to enhance swing mechanics while avoiding common back and knee issues.

A severe HIV outbreak in rural Indiana has infected 142 people, primarily linked to an opioid epidemic. The crisis has been exacerbated by a lack of medical resources, with only one infectious disease doctor serving the area. State officials have expanded needle exchange programs and sent health volunteers to combat the spread of disease in isolated communities.

The "Cheryl's birthday" logic problem went viral after being posted by a Singapore TV host, challenging high school students to deduce the correct date from a list of 10 possibilities using a conversation between two friends. The puzzle, which originated from the Singapore and Asian Schools Math Olympiad, has sparked widespread debate, with major publications like The New York Times and The Washington Post offering solutions, though the internet remains divided on the correct answer.

Mary Doyle Keefe, the model for Norman Rockwell's iconic "Rosie the Riveter," died at age 92. The 19-year-old Keefe posed for the famous 1943 Saturday Evening Post cover, where Rockwell transformed her slight frame into the era's symbol of women working during World War II.

Acetaminophen, the main ingredient in Tylenol, most forms of Midol and more than 600 other medicines, reduces not only pain but pleasure, acting as an "all-purpose emotion reliever" that blunts the range of feelings experienced. Researchers found that participants rated both pleasant and negative images less extremely under the drug's influence, often without realizing the change in their judgment.

A 17-year-old cancer patient, Cassandra C., has completed her chemotherapy treatment and been discharged from Connecticut Children's Medical Center after nearly a year of court-ordered custody. The legal battle, which centered on whether she could refuse life-saving treatment, concluded with a judge denying her attorney's request for release, citing she was no longer at "imminent harm." Now that her treatment is complete, the temporary order of custody has ended, and her attorney hailed the "happy outcome" as a victory for the state's interest in saving her life.

Chief Justice John Roberts is poised at the center of a landmark case that could establish a constitutional right to same-sex marriage nationwide. While Roberts, a conservative appointed by George W. Bush, has a history of dissenting on gay rights cases, both advocates and conservatives are watching closely to see if he will break precedent to rule in favor of marriage equality. The decision could cement Roberts' legacy, as a vote for same-sex couples would likely disappoint conservative allies who fear it would mirror his 2016 Obamacare vote.

The CDC and USDA held a press conference to discuss preparations for the latest bird flu outbreak, which is described as the worst since the 1980s. The risk to humans is low, the food supply is safe, and the CDC is monitoring at least 100 people who have worked with sick birds. While the virus does not spread through eating chickens or eggs, health leaders in Iowa said more than 5 million hens would have to be euthanized after bird flu was detected at a commercial laying facility there.

The earthquake caused significant damage to Kathmandu's historic pagodas, destroying the Shiva and Narayan temple pagodas that dominated Durbar Square and had served as public platforms for Hindu processions. While many structures crumbled or were smothered under wooden beams, others, particularly red brick shrines and the Shiva-Parvati temple house, surprisingly little damage and remained standing. A woman named her find the "Hallelujah Diamond" after discovering a 3.69-carat gem at Crater of Diamonds State Park following a prayer. The park, which allows visitors to dig for diamonds for a small fee, is the only public site in the world where the public can keep found gems. The discovery marks the largest find at the park this year and adds to the more than 75,000 diamonds discovered since 1906.

A powerful 7.9 magnitude earthquake struck Nepal, causing widespread destruction and raising fears of a rising death toll. The disaster was triggered by the Indian plate sliding underneath the Himalayas at a rate of 1.8 inches per year, with experts warning the casualty count could rise to match the 1934 earthquake that killed 10,000 people. Rescue efforts are hampered by avalanches on Mount Everest, and the event shares tragic similarities with the 2010 Haiti earthquake despite differences in magnitude.

Ben Powers, best known for his role as Keith Anderson on "Good Times," has died at age 64. He joined the cast in the show's final season in 1978-79 and played a professional football player who married Thelma. His family announced his death on April 6 in New Bedford, Mass., though no cause of death was revealed.

The journey to Gorkha reveals harrowing terrain and limited damage, but the town's hospital is overwhelmed, treating patients on dusty concrete floors with makeshift stretchers. Rescue workers face immense challenges reaching remote areas, as the facility serves only as a transit point due to a severe lack of ambulances and medical resources.

Photographer Ken Hermann spent about 10 days at Kolkata's Malik Ghat wholesale flower market to create his project "Flower Man." Despite challenges like language barriers, extreme heat, and the chaotic market atmosphere, Hermann focused on flower sellers willing to be photographed, capturing them by the the Hooghly River with a surreal, overexposed lighting style. He aimed to portray both male and female sellers, though many females declined participation, seeking to highlight the people behind the petals against a backdrop of Kolkata's bustling trade.

A Texas A&M professor threatened to fail his entire class after accusing students of cheating, lying, and "backstabbing," sparking a viral backlash online. The professor stood by his actions despite the intense media scrutiny, fearing professional repercussions.

A crowd gathers at Tokyo's Mitsukoshi Department Store to witness Aiko Chihira, an android designed to resemble a real 32-year-old woman. The robot, manufactured by Toshiba, can move, speak in sign language, and sing, marking a shift toward automation in Japan's service industry. Despite concerns from veteran staff, experts suggest robots like Chihira could soon replace humans due to the nation's shrinking workforce and aging population.

Lewis Hamilton dominated the Chinese Grand Prix, taking pole position and flag-to-flag victory under sunny skies, while his teammate Nico Rosberg claimed he was ruined by Hamilton's slow driving. The win narrowed Rosberg's championship lead to 13 points, with Sebastian Vettel finishing third for Ferrari. Rosberg expressed frustration over the team orders, insisting Hamilton's pace cost him time, though Hamilton maintained it was his job to bring the car home.

Richard Dysart, the acclaimed actor known for his role as Leland McKenzie on "L.A. Law," has died at age 86. He passed away at his home in Santa Monica after a brief illness, leaving behind a legacy of notable stage and screen work.

A longtime friend of Joni Mitchell has filed a legal petition seeking to be named the singer-songwriter's conservator. Mitchell, who was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997, was taken to UCLA Medical Center a month ago after being found unconscious in her home. E! will air a new documentary series this summer about Bruce Jenner's transition from male to female, premiering on July 26. The eight-part series will offer an unfiltered look at Jenner's relationships with his former wife Kris, his children, and his role within the transgender community, following his highly public announcement of his identity.

Kim Jong-unak's planned visit to Moscow for the World War II anniversary was canceled at the last minute, with Russia citing "North Korean domestic affairs." While the exact reason remains unclear, reports suggest Kim may fear instability at home, especially following reports that he executed 15 senior officials this year, including a vice chairman, for seemingly trivial objections like design changes.

Corion Colleges' closure of all 28 campuses marks a significant victory in the fight against predatory for-profit colleges, which have left students burdened with high debt and questionable degrees. Freddie Gray was arrested by Baltimore police on April 12 and fell into a coma shortly after being placed in a police van, dying a week later. Police released a detailed timeline stating Gray was placed in leg restraints and asked for medical attention, though an autopsy found no evidence of officer force being used against him. The events surrounding Gray's encounter with police remain unclear, though officials are investigating whether warnings were missed or if earlier action was needed.

Maickel Melamed, a 39-year-old with muscular dystrophy, completed the Boston Marathon just before 5 a.m. Tuesday, finishing the race nearly 20 hours after it began. His perseverance was celebrated by crowds and online fans, who viewed the event as a symbol of strength and unity less than two weeks after the convicted jury verdict regarding the 2013 Boston bombings.

Volvo will begin exporting vehicles made in a factory in southwest China to the United States next month, marking the first time Chinese-built passenger cars will roll into American showrooms. Geely Automobile, which bought Volvo in 2010, is seeking to prove that a Chinese company can manage a global auto brand. CEO Håkan Samuelsson emphasized that quality remains consistent regardless of where the cars are produced, downplaying concerns about quality for U.S. consumers.

Christopher Scarver killed Jeffrey Dahmer at Columbia Correctional Institution in 1994 because Dahmer's "creppy sense of humor" -- which included turning prison food into fake limbs covered with ketchup to resemble blood -- unnified Scarver. Scarver stated he attacked Dahmer and another inmate, Jesse Anderson with a metal bar from a weight room after an alteration while they were together unsupervised on a work detail.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has canceled his upcoming visit to Moscow to commemorate the World War II anniversary, citing domestic affairs. The trip was highly anticipated as it would have marked Kim's first official foreign trip since taking leadership in late 2011 and included planned meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The decision comes amid reports from South Korean intelligence that Kim is ruling with an "iron fist" after executing roughly 15 senior officials this year.

Google's Waze app, acquired in 2013, uses its "traffic cop" feature to pinpoint the real-time locations of police officers, posing a significant risk to their safety. While Google claims the app contributes to the "common good" of road safety, its use has enabled individuals to locate and target officers, as seen in the ambush killings of New York officers Ramos and Liu last December. It highlights specific instances, such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, and raises questions about potential influence on policy decisions, like the Keystone XL pipeline analysis. In Shanghai, rising car prices and license plate lotteries make vehicle ownership a challenge for young professionals like Li Lifei, who has waited six months to secure a Volkswagen license without success. The recent auction saw a plate sell for 80,600 yuan, roughly three times the cost of a basic Chinese car, prompting some affluent residents to abandon car ownership altogether. While hybrid and electric vehicles are presented as a potential solution, infrastructure remains limited and many still prefer traditional gasoline cars despite the growing market.

Rrioting in Baltimore was partly inspired by the "The Purge" movies, where social media rumors of a "purge" led by high school students caused chaos at a mall and elsewhere. The unrest began after the death of Freddie Gray, a man injured while in police custody, which sparked initially peaceful protests that turned violent.

Tanka Maya Sitoula survived 36 hours trapped under rubble after her five-story building collapsed during the Nepal earthquake, escaping with a beam protecting her. Her husband Mahendra called her for 18 hours before a 18-hour rescue effort by an Indian team finally freed her. The rescue was remarkably successful, with officials noting her upbeat survival as unlikely for others still trapped beneath the debris.

A CNN investigation reveals that hidden cameras placed in baggage handling areas at major airports have caught workers stealing from passengers' luggage. The analysis of TSA claims from 2010 to 2014 shows over 30,000 reports of missing items, mostly occurring in checked bags, with JFK, L.A., Orlando, and Miami topping the lists for theft. In response, Miami-Dade police have arrested 31 handlers since 2012 and implemented hidden cameras to proactively stop the rising issue of pilfering.

C-SPAN's live telecast of the White House Correspondents' Association dinner featured President Barack Obama and Cecily Strong, with Obama delivering sharp political jokes and Strong addressing the upcoming 2016 election. The event highlighted a "warmly American exercise in tolerance and good humor" despite a "tough room," serving as a notable moment for press freedom and presidential comedy.

Lifetime has greenlit a follow-up TV movie, "The Unauthorized Full House Story," which will explore the cast's on-screen family dynamic and the complicated realities of their lives outside the series. The project will be produced by the team behind the "Unauthorized Saved by the Bell" movie, with Ron McGhee writing the script. Production is set to begin immediately, though an air date has yet to be determined.

Chile's Calbuco Volcano erupted a third time on Thursday, producing an extensive ash plume that forced the evacuation of over 1,500 people. The event was described as less severe than the previous two eruptions, though authorities maintained seismic activity remained steady. Residents remain within a 12-mile exclusion zone as ash spread reached Argentina and blanketed local areas with gray debris up to two feet deep.

"Furious 7" serves as a bittersweet tribute to Paul Walker, blending high-octane, visceral action sequences with genuine emotion, though critics note the stunts often defy logic. The film succeeds in honoring the late star while delivering the signature franchise chaos.

"Avengers: Age of Ultron" struggles to recapture the surprise of its predecessor but leans heavily on familiar spectacle, with critics noting that some action scenes feel lackluster and the resolution could have been more complex. Despite these flaws, the film remains a successful crowd-pleaser poised to sh billion-dollar records internationally, cementing Marvel's enduring appeal.

A 14-year-old girl was returned to Mexico from Texas after DNA tests confirmed she was not related to a woman who claimed she was her daughter. Mexican federal police seized Alondra Luna Nuñez from her school based on a mistaken identity claim, but she was later sent to the U.S. where testing proved she belonged to her biological parents. The case began when a Houston woman claimed the girl had been illegally taken to Mexico, but authorities ultimately confirmed Alondra was not her daughter.

Michelle Keegan was named the world's sexiest woman by FHM, beating out Kendall Jenner and Jennifer Lawrence. The 27-year-old "Coronation Street" actress has been featured on the magazine's annual list, which hits newsstands on April 30.

Lois Lilienstein, co-star of the 1980s preschool show "Sharon, Lois & Bram's Elephant Show," has died at age 78 after a rare form of cancer. Her son confirmed she passed away peacefully in Toronto, noting she had known of her diagnosis before death. The "Sharon, Lois & Bram" trio became icons to children all across North America through various programs and specials.

Renowned cinematographer Andrew Lesnie, who won an Oscar for his work on "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy, has died at age 59 after a heart attack. He was a frequent collaborator with director Peter Jackson, lensing the "Hobbit" films and "King Kong" (2005), and recently completed Russell Crowe's directorial debut, "The Water Diviner."

Justin Timberlake and Jessica Biel have welcomed their first child, a son named Silas Randall Timberlake. The couple announced the arrival of the baby, whose name honors Timberlake's late grandfather and father, in statements to People. This marks the first child for the couple, who announced the pregnancy back in January.

Johnny Kemp, the R&B singer behind the 1988 hit "Just Got Paid," died this week after drowning at a beach in Montego Bay, Jamaica. He was 54 or 55 years old and was scheduled to perform at the Tom Joyner Foundation Fantastic Voyage Cruise before his death. Tributes from fellow artists like Chris Kirkpatrick and Samuel L. Jackson called him a "humble and kind spirit."

Walmart, Target, and Koch Industries have joined the movement to "ban the box," removing criminal history questions from initial job applications to focus on skills and qualifications instead. These "fair-chance" hiring reforms aim to reduce recidivism and racial disparities, as advocates argue that 70 million Americans with records face systemic barriers to employment. The policies are gaining traction across the political spectrum, with 16 states and numerous local governments adopting these measures to help reintegrate millions of people into the labor market.

The Supreme Court heard arguments regarding same-sex marriage, where Justice Gorsburg highlighted the historical evolution of marriage, noting it transitioned from a "dominant and subordinate" dynamic where the husband controlled the couple's domicile. Attorney Mary Bonauto countered that for centuries, marriage was a coverture system absorbing a woman's legal identity into her husband's. Justice Thomas, the likely swing vote, referenced the " nobility and sacredness of marriage," arguing its definition has not changed, while noting the historical illegality of interracial marriage bans introduced in 1661.

Kabul's streets reflect the legacy of America's longest war, where former NATO allies are now jobless and blacklisted, left isolated and fearing reprisals. Once valuable skills have abandoned them, they now sleep in market stalls while avoiding their families due to threats. Meanwhile, the city's population has swollen five times its pre-war size, with once-privileged foreigner neighborhoods now empty as Afghans reclaim streets previously held by contractors and NGO workers.

The quaint town of Dunblane, Scotland, was set abuzz by the wedding of tennis legend Andy Murray to his long-term girlfriend, Kim Sears. Saturday's event -- dubbed "the royal wedding of Scotland" -- took place at Dunblane Cathedral, with cheering crowds spilling onto the streets to support their home-grown talent. The couple met at the U.S. Open in 2005 and got engaged in November last year, but any plans for a honeymoon have been put on hold as the world number three returns to tournament action next week.

Photographer Simon Brann Thorpe's "Toy Soldiers" project uses toy-like plastic figurines placed in the harsh landscape of Western Sahara to create a visual metaphor for the region's ongoing conflict. Thorpe's work highlights the 40-year anniversary of war in Western Sahara, where a ceasefire in 1991 left the population split between Moroccan-occupied territory and refugee camps in Algeria. After a five-week production process involving the Polisario Front military, Thorpe hopes his images provoke reflection on how war imagery is consumed amid diminishing attention spans.

Percy Sledge, the R&B belter whose biggest hit, "When a Man Loves a Woman," became a cornerstone of soul music, died Tuesday at the age of 73. Sledge died of natural causes in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, while in hospice care for cancer. His 1966 classic, which hit No. 1 on the charts, became a standard covered by numerous artists and featured on several movie soundtracks.

Southwest Airlines topped the study, offering the most award tickets and the highest percentage of award seats, while JetBlue ranked lowest with the fewest award seats and the fewest number of award tickets. Delta, United, and American Airlines followed in second through fourth place. Consumer Reports notes that award tickets aren't free but cost miles built into purchases, urging consumers to book award travel carefully to maximize value.

In 2011, 16-year-old Gulnaz was raped by her cousin's husband, Asadullah, and was subsequently imprisoned for adultery. After international outrage, President Hamid Karzai pardoned her, but to survive societal shame, she was pressured into marrying her attacker. The article highlights how this "cohabitation" solution—driven by conservative traditions and government pressure—perentrudes the idea that women's rights in Afghanistan remain fundamentally compromised despite international investment.

Freddie Gray died one week after his arrest in Baltimore, but the circumstances of his death remain unclear, with his family's attorney alleging a police cover-up and claiming Gray was injured and placed in a coma before dying after surgery. The incident has reignited national debate over policing, coming amid recent deaths like Michael Brown in Ferguson, as Baltimore protesters demand transparency amid ongoing criminal investigations.

A New York jury is still deliberating the fate of Pedro Hernandez, who confessed to killing 6-year-old Etan Patz in 1979 but claims his memory is unreliable due to mental illness. Despite a judge ruling his confession admissible, the jury has deadlocked twice, leaving the grieving parents to wait over 35 years for justice. The case has been further complicated by the fact that Hernandez’s mental state and the validity of his confession remain central points of the trial.

A quadruple rainbow over New York was captured by Amanda Curtis, who initially thought she saw only one before realizing there were four. The phenomenon was explained as a "double rainbow reflected in a smooth body of water," sparking viral excitement online.

Japan's space agency announced plans to land an unmanned rover on the moon by 2018, joining an elite club of nations who have explored Earth's satellite. The mission aims to perfect soft-landing technologies and utilize face recognition software to identify craters, with an estimated cost of ¥10 to ¥15 billion. Despite narrowly missing the world record, their score of 94.196 was a full 10 percentage points clear of the second-place finisher. The weekend's events in Las Vegas were also notable for younger riders, with 19-year-old Bertrem Allen taking bronze in jumping and Laura Graves improving to fourth in Dressage.

The world's top showjumping and dressage horses have arrived in Las Vegas for the World Cup Finals, traveling in style via Qatar Airways with dedicated care for their every needs. The event, hosted at the Thomas & Mack Center with a $8 million budget and expected 80,000 fans, aims to raise the sport's profile in the U.S. by blending traditional equestrian competition with high-profile Vegas entertainment, featuring stars like Germany's Daniel Deusser and Beezie Madden competing for prestigious titles.

An Israeli couple in Kathmandu is anxiously awaiting the birth of their unborn child via surrogate mother Nafisa Shaje, as a devastating earthquake endangers the mother and baby. The father, Ronen Ziv, fears the surrogate cannot receive the necessary medical care for a safe delivery amid collapsed hospitals and severe injury shortages. He is hoping to relocate the mother to Israel for proper care, but the imminent due date makes such travel precally impossible.

In 1944, 16-year-old Yong Soo Lee was lured into a train and ship transport to Taiwan, where she and other girls were forced into sexual slavery for a year, suffering severe beatings, torture, and disease. These "comfort women" from across Asia suffered unimaginable physical, emotional, and psychological trauma during World War II. Despite repeated Japanese government attempts to deny or rewrite the history, Rep. [Name] and colleagues continue urging a clear, unequivocal apology and historical responsibility for these victims.

Chad Bernstein founded "Guitars Over Guns" to provide free music instruction and mentorship to at-risk students in Miami's poorest communities, credencing a 90% increase in academic performance and school attendance. The program aims to give children a sense of identity and belonging through music, pairing them with professional musicians to foster growth and creativity.

Two CNN Heroes in Kathmandu, Nepal, are struggling in the aftermath of the earthquake. Anuradha Koirala, who rescues victims of sex trafficking, houses 425 girls in a rehabilitation center that has been rendered unsafe, forcing them to sleep outdoors amid aftershocks and fears of cholera. Meanwhile, Pushpa Basnet's orphanage and construction project suffered extensive damage, leaving the children she cares for living in fear and makeshift shelters with limited resources.

NPR's report on the Baltimore unrest sparked controversy by suggesting African-Americans were targeting Asian-owned businesses, a claim echoed after previous riots. However, experts note this narrative often misinterprets economic and social volatility as racial targeting, directing blame away from deeper structural inequalities. As Jennifer Lee observes, media focus on interminority conflict distracts from the root causes of poverty and disadvantage in urban communities.

Jordan Spieth won the Masters Tournament in a dominant performance, becoming the second-youngest winner in history and dedicating the victory to his late sister Ellie. Despite the pressure of professional golf, Spieth credited his 14-year-old sister with providing him perspective and perspective, stating she is "the most special part of our family" and "my biggest supporter." He expressed that her influence helps him realize that frustrations on a round of golf are "really secondary," and he looked forward to getting back to her and letting her try on the green jacket.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued over two months after his sailboat capsided in the Atlantic Ocean. The young sailor survived by rationing food and water, collecting rain by catching it in his laundry, and fishing by using his clothing as bait. His father, Frank Jordan, expressed deep relief upon learning of his son's survival, crediting his strength and faith as key factors in his endurance.

A decade ago, support for same-sex marriage among religious Americans was under 30%, but by 2014 it had climbed to 47%, surpassing the 45% opposition. This dramatic shift, driven by a survey of 40,000 adults, suggests the Supreme Court may soon issue a landmark ruling legalizing same-sex marriage nationwide.

California Governor Jerry Brown has issued mandatory statewide water restrictions to end the fourth-year drought, acknowledging that population and economic growth must respect planetary limits. The measures target urban use but exclude dominant agricultural consumers, highlighting a need for long-term reform as the drought is expected to worsen due to climate change. The crisis holds global significance, mirroring unsustainable water practices in regions like the Indian subcontinent and contributing to conflict in Syria, underscoring that water scarcity is a worldwide challenge intensified by human-induced climate change.

Millennials are redefining marriage, prioritizing personal success and travel over traditional wedlock, with many viewing singledhood as a valid alternative to the financial and social pressures of the past. Despite a backdrop of rising divorce rates and economic concerns, this generation views marriage as a choice made for happiness rather than a mandatory milestone, valuing independence and experience over societal expectations.

Anthony Sideri's life spiraled downward after he began using heroin, transitioning from painkiller abuse before he had just robbed a bank to fuel his addiction. He hit rock bottom in a jail bathroom in July 2007, realizing he was "going to die" after nearly fatally withdrawing from the drug. Nearly eight years later, Sideri reflects on his addiction like it was "another person's life," having lost his eligibility to play sports and his job, family, and car over the course of his dependency.

A crisis of migrant deaths in the Mediterranean has suddenly focused global attention, though the tragedy has brewed for years. In Catania, Sicily, locals fear the island cannot absorb the influx, as EU officials warn up to a million migrants could arrive this year alone. While some Italians demand borders remain open, far others are losing patience, regional governments have declared they will no longer accept new arrivals.

NASA's Messenger probe intentionally crashed into Mercury on Thursday after running out of fuel, ending its 11-year mission. The impact occurred on the planet's far side, creating a crater and providing scientists with valuable data on Mercury's composition and polar ice. While the mission is over, researchers will spend years analyzing the probe's findings, and Mercury remains visible to the naked eye in the night sky until the end of May.

Chile's Calbuco Volcano erupted twice in 24 hours, spewing ash and lava that prompted mass evacuations. Officials established a 12-mile exclusion zone and warned of potential further activity, as airborne ash reached altitudes of 12,000 feet and rising river levels forced thousands to flee. The situation remains relatively calm, though residents are anxious about a possible third eruption.

Erica Kinsman has filed a lawsuit against Jameis Winston, accusing him of rape that occurred in December 2012. The case was previously declined for criminal charges, and Winston has maintained the sex was consensual. The lawsuit alleges sexual battery and false imprisonment, with Kinsman's attorney stating they are seeking to clear her name ahead of Winston's upcoming NFL draft.

The Italian Coast Guard vessel Calabrese, based out of Lampedusa, routinely patrols the Mediterranean to rescue migrants in distress. During a routine patrol, the crew encountered a small boat that appeared to be a fishing vessel but was actually overloaded with people, prompting a standard safety check. The mission highlighted the crew's ongoing trauma from past disasters, like the 2013 shipwreck that claimed over 350 lives, underscining the high cost of their daily duties.

According to a South Korean lawmaker, Kim Jong Un has ordered the execution of about 15 senior officials this year, citing dissatisfaction with programs and design changes. The National Intelligence Service reports Kim has executed a total of 17, 10, and 41 officials in 2012, 2013, and 2014 respectively. The intelligence suggests Kim rules authoritatively, punishing those who object to his decisions, as North Korea remains one of the most closed societies in the world.

Taylor Swift revealed on Thursday that her mother, Andrea Swift, has been diagnosed with cancer. The singer requested keeping the details of her mother's condition and treatment plans private, though she shared the news to ease her own and her brother's worries. In response, Swift urged her fans to ensure their own parents undergo regular cancer screenings, emphasizing that early detection can lead to a better outcome.

At least two people were detained in Baltimore after protests over Freddie Gray's death turned confrontational. Demonstrators and police clashed, with some shouting "Back up!" and surrounding a police car, while the Baltimore Police Department cited disorderly conduct and destruction of property. The attorney for the Gray family criticized the lack of information, and a police union's "lynch mob" comparison drew sharp criticism rooted in the history of racial violence.

Bikram Choudhury, the founder of the "hot yoga" movement, faces sexual assault allegations from six former students, prompting many studios to drop his name. The 93-year-old guru denies the claims, insisting he would never assault women, while accusers like Sarah Baughn say he has manipulated and lied to hide his actions. With civil lawsuits filed and police declining to pursue charges, the once-celebrated icon's brand is collapsing as his legacy crumbles under accusations of rape and misconduct.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi represent the economic trajectories of the world's two most populous nations. While Modi celebrates India's space program and pushes "Make in India" to fast-track economic growth, Xi manages a slowing domestic economy through anti-corruption efforts. However, despite optimistic predictions that India could overtake China, experts argue India faces significant structural challenges—including infrastructure gaps and unemployment—that prevent it from rivaling China's established manufacturing might.

DARPA has successfully demonstrated that small-caliber "smart bullets" can hit moving and evading targets with extreme accuracy, potentially eliminating the need for expert marksmanship. The EXACTO program achieved this breakthrough by integrating guidance capabilities into a .50-caliber projectile, opening the door to future guided projectiles across all calibers. The technology is designed to enhance shooter accuracy at greater distances and ultimately improve the safety of American troops in the field.

Sarah Brady, a prominent gun control advocate, died at 73 from pneumonia. She became an activist after her husband, James Brady—Ronald Reagan's press secretary—was shot in the 1981 assassination attempt. Together, she helped pass landmark legislation like the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, transforming tragedy into a lifelong campaign for safer gun laws.

The order comes following the Al-Shabaab attack at Garissa University College, which the Kenyan government claims was orchestrated by senior leader Mohamed Mohamud and exploits the Dadaab complex's "extensive terrorist network." Greenpeace activists have climbed aboard the Shell oil rig "Polar Pioneer" to protest the company's plans to drill in the Arctic. The action comes as the U.S. government recently lifted suspensions on oil and gas leases in the Chukchi Sea, potentially allowing Shell to begin drilling in the Alaskan Arctic within 100 days.

In Russia's tightly controlled political landscape, President Vladimir Putin hosts an annual live Q&A session where he fields carefully vetted questions from the public. The event, which typically lasts several hours, serves as a highly choreographed platform for the leader to address domestic and foreign issues, rather than offering a genuine venue for critical dissent. Critics view the session as a staged exercise in "managed democracy" rather than a conduit for authentic public influence.

Saudi airstrikes targeting a Yemeni military base on Tuesday inadvertently hit a nearby school, killing at least three students and injuring several others. The attack occurred as the schoolchildren were heading to their lunch break, and the school was located roughly 500 meters from the intended military target. The incident highlights the broader chaos in Yemen, where civilians are increasingly caught in the crossfire of fighting that has killed hundreds in less than two weeks.

Izzat Ibrahim al-Douri, a former top deputy to Saddam Hussein and a key figure in Sunni extremist groups, was killed in a security operation in Iraq. The operation, involving Iraqi security forces and Shia militia, took place in the Hamrin Mountains, and al-Douri was identified through DNA samples. The U.S. military is aware of the reports but has not yet evaluated further information regarding the death of the former regime official.

The Solar Impulse 2 has been grounded in Chongqing, China, due to unfavorable weather conditions, extending what was supposed to be an overnight stop into a two-and-half-week layover. The pilots and team are waiting for improved wind conditions before attempting the leg across the Pacific Ocean to Hawaii.

ISIS has released official documents detailing its governance in territories it controls, including birth certificates, vaccination schedules, and university reopenings. The group enforces a strict interpretation of Islamic law, banning subjects like archaeology and democracy while permitting girls' education and running a health department that allows vaccinations, distinguishing it from groups like the Taliban.

Five Chinese feminists were released on bail after being detained just before International Women's Day, but their families expressed mixed emotions as the case remains ongoing. The plaintiff, Paul Nungesser, argues the university failed its legal and contractual obligation to protect him after his name was cleared in a disciplinary hearing.

President Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro shook hands at a dinner in Panama City, marking the first high-level U.C. talks in over five decades. The meeting signifies a major shift in U.S.-Cuba relations, as Obama is expected to remove Cuba from the terrorism list to further normalize ties. Nepal is currently recovering from two major earthquakes and a mudslide, with many parts of the country struggling daily. To help those affected, several vetted organizations are accepting donations, including the Red Cross, ActionAid, Catholic Relief Services, and World Vision.

SpaceX successfully launched a Dragon cargo spacecraft to the International Space Station, but the attempt to land the Falcon 9 rocket booster on a floating barge failed, as the stage tipped over and exploded upon impact. Elon Musk later clarified that while the rocket landed successfully, it tipped over during the process. The Dragon spacecraft is set to deliver over 4,300 pounds of supplies and science experiments to the station, where the crew will spend about five weeks unpacking the cargo before sending it back to Earth via a Pacific Ocean splashdown.

The Supreme Court heard historic arguments on the constitutionality of same-sex marriage, with Justices appearing divided on whether the issue should be decided by the states or the judiciary. Justice Anthony Kennedy, the court's pivotal vote, seemed poised to play a key role, expressing concern over the traditional definition of marriage while also signaling sympathy toward same-sex couples' desire for "dignity." Chief Justice John Roberts voiced hesitation, suggesting that letting the debate to individual states could "close minds" and impact how the new institution of marriage is accepted.

The death of Freddie Gray following his arrest on a weapons charge has sparked protests and accusations of police brutality, with the exact cause of his spinal cord injury remaining unclear. While police have stated Gray was placed in a van without a seatbelt and requested medical attention, the specific events inside the van and why he screamed remain unknown. Six officers have been suspended as part of the standard procedure following an "in-custody death," but the investigation into what caused Gray's injury continues.

The UN is appealing for $174 million to aid 192,000 Nigerian refugees fleeing Boko Haram's six-year insurgency into neighboring nations. The militants' attacks on schools and villages have killed thousands and kidnapped over 200 girls, leaving many displaced children unable to attend school or separated from their parents. Aid agencies are scrambling to provide clean water, shelter, food, and mental health support, as adequate funding is crucial to improve living conditions for the refugees.

A Michigan police officer was charged with assault and mistreatment of a prisoner after video showed him beating a motorist during a traffic stop. The motorist was cleared of all drug charges, and the police chief resigned following the incident. Prosecutors are continuing to investigate the case as the motorist and his attorney maintain to vigorously contest the officer's actions.

The U.S. Navy is developing unmanned drone ships like the ACTUV to counter the expanding submarine capabilities of China and other nations. Initiated by DARPA, these autonomous vessels are designed to independently track enemy diesel-electric submarines over long distances, with a prototype already in production and the Navy eyeing further development by 2018.

Nobel laureate Günter Grass, the author of the acclaimed novel "The Tin Drum," has died at the age of 87. His publisher confirmed his death in a clinic in Lübeck, noting he had been in poor health over the weekend. Grass, known for his innovative use of child narrators, remained a controversial figure in his later years for his public statements regarding the Holocaust and Israel.

Feiden Santana recorded a South Carolina police officer fatally shooting a fleeing, unarmed man, Walter Scott, after being told by another officer to stop using his phone. The video evidence led to the officer's firing and murder charge, though Santana initially feared for his life before coming forward. Santana recalled that Walter Scott was running away when he began recording, and he believes Scott was trying to get away from the officer, Michael Slager, who used a Taser against him.

A magnitude-7.8 earthquake near Kathmandu flattened homes and temples, killing over 1,800 people and injuring thousands, with the death toll expected to rise as rescue efforts continue. The quake triggered avalanches on Mount Everest and widespread destruction across rural Nepal, where 80% of houses were leveled, leaving millions displaced and huddling in the cold rain. Rescue crews are searching through rubble for survivors as aftershocks persist, with officials confirming at least 34 deaths in neighboring India and 13 in Tibet.

A former Japanese school principal, Yuhei Takashima, was arrested for paying for sex with over 12,000 women, including miners as young as 13 or 14, during trips to the Philippines. Police seized over 147,600 photos and 400 albums from his residence, uncovering a case that began in 1988. Takashima, now 64, faces criminal charges, with authorities believing the abuse occurred in Manila in January 2014.

The alleged ringleader, Gilbert "Toby" Curtsinger, a Buffalo Trace employee, faces charges alongside his wife. The investigation, which took years cold, culminated after a tip led authorities to recover stolen barrels and steroids from Curtsinger's home.

Since then, CyArk, founded by engineer Ben Kacyra, has used groundbreaking laser scanning technology to digitally preserve endangered historical architecture, ensuring that accurate digital versions of world heritage sites survive for future reconstruction and education, even despite threats like war and natural disasters.
